title: Module 3 · IV Room and USP 797
intro: Your yearly sterile compounding competency (garbing, fingertip testing, media fill), rooms and air, cleaning, BUDs, vials, hazardous drugs, vincristine, diluent catches, parenteral nutrition and the final check.

cases.title: Your sterile compounding competency
cases.stem: Before you can compound alone in the IV room, you must pass the sterile compounding competency. You will repeat parts of it on a schedule as long as you work there.

steps.q: What does the competency include?

options.t: Training plus a knowledge test
options.why: Initially, then at least every 12 months.

options.t: Garbing and hand hygiene with gloved fingertip sampling
Media fill, fingertip sampling and a surface sample
Viable air sampling of the room by the compounder
options.why: Air sampling is facility monitoring (every 6 months), not a personnel competency.

options.t: Hood certification performed by the compounder
options.why: Certification is done by a qualified certifier every 6 months.

steps.q: Before compounding alone the first time, how many gloved fingertip tests must you pass after garbing, and what result passes?

options.t: Three times, each with zero CFU
options.why: Initial garbing qualification: action level above 0 CFU.

options.t: Three times, each with 3 CFU or fewer
options.why: Above 3 CFU is the action level after a media fill, not after garbing.

options.t: Once, with zero CFU
options.why: Initial qualification needs three consecutive passes.

options.t: Once, with 3 CFU or fewer
options.why: Mixes the media fill action level with a single test.

steps.teach: Zero growth means your gloves stayed clean while you garbed. That is the point of the whole sequence.
steps.where: St. Mary's IV room competency SOP and the IV room supervisor or trainer.

steps.q: After the media fill test, the gloved fingertip action level is:

options.t: More than 3 CFU total fails
More than 0 CFU total fails
options.why: That is the action level after garbing.

options.t: More than 1 CFU per hand fails
More than 10 CFU total fails

steps.q: How often must you repeat garbing and aseptic manipulation competency if you compound Category 1 and 2 CSPs?

options.t: At least every 6 months
At least every 3 months
options.why: Every 3 months applies to Category 3 compounders.

options.t: At least every 12 months
options.why: 12 months is the training and knowledge test cycle (and supervisors who do not compound).

options.t: At least every 24 months
options.why: No USP 797 competency runs every 2 years.

cases.pearl: **Garb: 3 passes at 0 CFU to start. Media fill fingertip: above 3 CFU fails. Repeat every 6 months (Cat 1 and 2), training every 12 months.**

cases.title: Garbing in the right order
cases.stem: You walk into the ante room to garb.

steps.q: What is the principle behind the garbing order?

options.t: Dirtiest to cleanest
options.why: Shoe and hair covers before washing.

options.t: Cleanest to dirtiest
Top of the body to the bottom
Any order, as long as gloves go on last
options.why: Order matters to avoid touching dirty items with clean hands.

steps.q: Put these in order: gown, shoe covers, wash hands, sterile gloves, hair cover and face mask.

options.t: Shoe covers, hair cover, mask, wash, gown, sterile gloves
Wash, shoe covers, hair cover, mask, gown, sterile gloves
options.why: Touching shoe covers after washing recontaminates hands.

options.t: Shoe covers, hair cover, mask, gown, wash, sterile gloves
options.why: The gown goes on after washing.

options.t: Hair cover, mask, wash, gown, shoe covers, sterile gloves
options.why: Shoe covers after the gown recontaminate hands and gown.

steps.teach: Your SOP is the final word on the exact order and where the line of demarcation is.
steps.where: St. Mary's garbing SOP (posted in the ante room).

steps.q: How long is the hand wash?

options.t: At least 30 seconds, nails cleaned, to the elbows
At least 15 seconds, hands and wrists only
At least 20 seconds, as in routine patient care
options.why: 20 seconds is general hand hygiene; compounding needs at least 30.

options.t: At least 2 minutes with a scrub brush
options.why: Brushes are not required and can damage skin.

steps.q: What do you use on your gloves during compounding?

options.t: Sterile 70% IPA, reapplied often, allowed to dry
Nonsterile 70% IPA, since gloves are already sterile
options.why: Sterile IPA is required inside ISO 5.

options.t: Alcohol based hand rub applied over the gloves
options.why: Hand rub is for bare hands before gloving.

options.t: Nothing once sterile gloves are on

cases.pearl: **Dirty to clean: shoes, hair, mask, wash 30 seconds, gown, sterile gloves, sterile IPA.**

cases.title: Media fill: what it proves
cases.stem: Your trainer hands you bags and vials of growth medium (soybean casein digest) instead of real drugs.

steps.q: What is the media fill test for?

options.t: Prove aseptic technique with growth medium
Test the hood's HEPA filter integrity
Measure particle counts in the buffer room
Check that the BUD on labels is correct

steps.q: After incubation the medium is cloudy (turbid). What does that mean?

options.t: Failure: retrain and repeat the whole competency
options.why: If any part fails, the whole aseptic assessment is repeated.

options.t: Normal: growth medium always turns cloudy
Failure: repeat only the fingertip sample
options.why: The whole aseptic manipulation assessment is repeated.

options.t: Pass, if fewer than 3 units are cloudy
options.why: Any turbid unit is a failure.

steps.q: How is a media fill usually incubated under the 2023 chapter?

options.t: 20 to 25 °C and 30 to 35 °C, 7 days each
30 to 35 °C only, for 48 to 72 hours
options.why: Resembles fingertip plate incubation, not media fill.

options.t: 2 to 8 °C, refrigerated, for 14 days
20 to 25 °C only, for 5 to 7 days

cases.pearl: **Media fill: copy your hardest work with growth medium. Clear = pass. Cloudy = fail and repeat everything.**

sources.t: USP General Chapter 797, Pharmaceutical Compounding: Sterile Preparations (2023 revision)

cases.title: Rooms, ISO classes and pressure
cases.stem: On your tour you see the hood, the buffer room and the ante room.

steps.q: Match the area to its ISO class.

options.t: Hood ISO 5; buffer ISO 7; ante ISO 8
options.why: Ante ISO 7 if it opens to a negative pressure buffer room.

options.t: Hood ISO 5; buffer ISO 8; ante ISO 7
Hood ISO 7; buffer ISO 7; ante ISO 8
Hood ISO 5; buffer ISO 5; ante ISO 7

steps.q: Which way should air flow between the buffer room and ante room for non hazardous compounding?

options.t: Buffer to ante (buffer positive, at least 0.02 inch)
Ante to buffer (buffer negative, 0.01 to 0.03 inch)
options.why: Negative pressure is for hazardous drug rooms (USP 800).

options.t: No airflow between rooms (equal pressure)
options.why: Pressure difference protects the buffer room.

options.t: Buffer to hallway, skipping the ante room
options.why: Air flows clean to less clean through the ante room.

steps.q: What is "first air"?

options.t: HEPA filtered air before it touches anything
Air in the ante room right after garbing
The first full air change of the shift
Room air drawn back into the HEPA filter
options.why: That air has already touched surfaces.

steps.teach: Most contamination in a working hood comes from the compounder blocking first air or touching critical sites.

cases.pearl: **ISO 5 hood, ISO 7 buffer, ISO 8 ante. Buffer positive. Never block first air.**

sources.t: USP General Chapter 797, Pharmaceutical Compounding: Sterile Preparations (2023 revision)
Florida DOH: USP 797 inspection checklist (2024)

cases.title: Environmental monitoring and certification
cases.stem: The IV room supervisor shows you the monitoring binder.

steps.q: How often are the hoods and cleanroom certified?

options.t: Every 6 months and after major repairs
Every 12 months and after major repairs
Every month and after major repairs
Every 3 months and after major repairs
options.why: 3 months is the Category 3 competency cycle.

steps.q: Under the 2023 chapter, how often is surface sampling done in classified areas and hoods?

options.t: At least monthly
At least every 6 months
options.why: 6 months is viable air sampling and certification.

options.t: At least weekly
At least every 12 months

steps.q: A surface sample from the hood work surface grows mold. What happens?

options.t: Investigate, sporicidal clean, resample, document
options.why: Any mold in ISO 5 needs action.

options.t: Ignore it if the count is under the action level
options.why: Mold in ISO 5 always needs investigation.

options.t: Clean with sterile IPA only and continue
Wait for the next 6 month certification

cases.pearl: **Certify every 6 months. Surface sample monthly. Air sample every 6 months.**

sources.t: USP General Chapter 797, Pharmaceutical Compounding: Sterile Preparations (2023 revision)
St. Mary's IV room SOPs, BUD policy and competency program (verify locally)

cases.title: Cleaning the hood
cases.stem: It is the start of your IV room shift.

steps.q: What three steps make up cleaning under USP 797?

options.t: Clean, disinfect, then apply sterile 70% IPA
Spray sterile IPA and wipe immediately
options.why: IPA alone does not clean residue; wiping too soon defeats contact time.

options.t: Disinfect first, then clean, then IPA
Sporicidal agent daily instead of cleaning
options.why: Sporicidal is at least monthly, on top of routine cleaning.

steps.q: Which direction do you clean the hood?

options.t: Top to bottom, back to front, away from HEPA
Front to back, moving toward the HEPA filter
options.why: Pushes dirt into the critical area.

options.t: Bottom to top, then back to front
Circles from the center of the work surface

steps.q: How often is a sporicidal agent used in the hood?

options.t: At least monthly (and if contamination suspected)
At least weekly, on the same day each week
At least every 6 months, at certification
options.why: 6 months is certification and air sampling.

options.t: Only after a positive surface sample result
options.why: It is scheduled, not only reactive.

cases.pearl: **Clean, disinfect, IPA. Top to bottom, back to front. Sporicidal monthly.**

sources.t: USP General Chapter 797, Pharmaceutical Compounding: Sterile Preparations (2023 revision)

cases.title: Immediate use in an emergency
cases.stem: During a code, a nurse needs an amiodarone infusion mixed outside the IV room.

steps.q: What are the immediate use rules?

options.t: 3 sterile products max; start within 4 hours
3 sterile products max; start within 12 hours
options.why: 12 hours is the Category 1 room temperature BUD.

options.t: 5 sterile products max; start within 4 hours
3 sterile products max; start within 1 hour
options.why: 1 hour applies to a single dose vial punctured outside ISO 5.

steps.q: Why is the window so short?

options.t: Made outside clean air: little time for growth
Amiodarone degrades within 4 hours
options.why: The limit is about sterility, not stability.

options.t: Code drugs are always given within 1 hour
Only pharmacists may compound beyond 4 hours

cases.pearl: **Immediate use: 3 products max, start within 4 hours.**

sources.t: USP General Chapter 797, Pharmaceutical Compounding: Sterile Preparations (2023 revision)

cases.title: Category 1 or Category 2?
cases.stem: You prepare cefazolin 2 g in 100 mL NS in a hood located in a segregated compounding area (not a cleanroom suite).

steps.q: What category is this, and what is the maximum BUD?

options.t: Category 1: 12 h room temp or 24 h refrigerated
options.why: A hood in a segregated area makes Category 1 only.

options.t: Category 2: 4 days room temp or 10 days refrigerated
Immediate use: 4 hours
options.why: It was made in a hood, not under immediate use rules.

options.t: Category 1: 24 h room temp or 48 h refrigerated

steps.q: The same bag made in the cleanroom suite from all sterile ingredients, no sterility test. Maximum BUD?

options.t: 4 days room temp, 10 days fridge, 45 days frozen
options.why: Sterile starting ingredients, no sterility test.

options.t: 1 day room temp, 4 days fridge, 45 days frozen
options.why: That is Category 2 with a nonsterile ingredient.

options.t: 30 days room temp, 45 days fridge, 60 days frozen
options.why: That requires a passed sterility test.

options.t: 12 hours room temp, 24 hours fridge

steps.q: If any starting ingredient is nonsterile (for example a bulk powder), the Category 2 BUD drops to:

options.t: 1 day room temp, 4 days fridge, 45 days frozen
4 days room temp, 10 days fridge, 45 days frozen
12 hours room temp, 24 hours fridge
No change; sterility of ingredients does not matter

steps.q: What also limits the BUD besides the USP category?

options.t: Chemical and physical stability of the drug
options.why: The BUD is the shorter of sterility and stability.

options.t: The manufacturer's expiration date on the vial
options.why: Vial expiration limits the vial, but the CSP BUD comes from USP limits and stability.

options.t: The patient's expected length of stay
The pump's programmed infusion time

cases.pearl: **Cat 1: 12 h room, 24 h fridge. Cat 2 sterile ingredients: 4 / 10 / 45 days. Always the shorter of sterility and stability.**

cases.title: Single dose and multiple dose vials
cases.stem: A single dose vial of ondansetron was punctured in the hood 6 hours ago. A multiple dose vial of insulin was opened 20 days ago.

steps.q: Can you use the single dose vial again?

options.t: Yes: up to 12 hours if punctured and kept in ISO 5
Yes: up to 28 days, like a multiple dose vial
options.why: 28 days is the multiple dose vial rule.

options.t: Yes: up to 1 hour only
options.why: 1 hour applies when punctured outside ISO 5.

options.t: No: single dose vials are always one entry only

steps.q: Can the multiple dose vial still be used?

options.t: Yes: 28 days after opening unless labeled otherwise
No: 14 days after opening is the limit
No: 12 hours after first puncture
options.why: That is the single dose vial rule.

options.t: Yes: until the manufacturer expiration date

cases.pearl: **Single dose vial: 12 h inside ISO 5, 1 h outside. Multiple dose vial: 28 days.**

sources.t: USP General Chapter 797, Pharmaceutical Compounding: Sterile Preparations (2023 revision)

cases.title: Hazardous drug compounding
cases.stem: An order arrives for cyclophosphamide, a NIOSH listed antineoplastic.

steps.q: Where is it compounded?

options.t: Containment hood in a negative pressure room
Laminar airflow hood in a positive pressure room
Containment hood in a positive pressure room
Any hood if the compounder wears double gloves

steps.q: What protective equipment do you wear?

options.t: Two pairs of ASTM D6978 chemotherapy gloves
A permeation resistant gown that closes in the back
A closed system transfer device when possible
options.why: Required for administration, recommended for compounding.

options.t: One pair of sterile nitrile exam gloves
A cloth lab coat over scrubs

steps.q: A nurse calls about a hazardous drug bag that leaked on the floor. What do you tell them?

options.t: Spill kit and full PPE; contain from outside in
Paper towels, then the regular trash bin
Pour bleach directly on it, then mop it up
options.why: Contain first with the spill kit.

options.t: Leave it for environmental services staff
options.why: Trained staff with PPE contain it.

cases.pearl: **Hazardous drugs: negative pressure, double chemo gloves, chemo gown, CSTD, spill kit.**

sources.t: USP General Chapter 800, Hazardous Drugs: Handling in Healthcare Settings
St. Mary's IV room SOPs, BUD policy and competency program (verify locally)

cases.title: Vincristine: the never event
cases.stem: A vincristine dose is ready to dispense. The oncology nurse asks for it in a syringe "to make it faster."

steps.q: How must vincristine be dispensed?

options.t: In a minibag, never a syringe
options.why: Intrathecal vincristine is almost always fatal; a minibag cannot connect to a spinal needle.

options.t: In a syringe labeled "For IV use only"
In a syringe with a non luer connector
In a syringe, kept in a separate bin from intrathecal drugs
options.why: Separation helps, but the minibag is the safeguard.

cases.call: Explain the reason calmly: "Vincristine is fatal if it is ever given into the spine, and the minibag makes that impossible. It is ready now in a minibag."

sources.t: ISMP: vincristine labeling and packaging changes to prevent wrong route (minibag dispensing)

cases.title: Diluent catches
cases.stem: Four orders are waiting for your final check.

steps.q: Which of these are diluent errors?

options.t: Phenytoin in D5W
options.why: Precipitates; NS only, 0.22 micron filter, max 50 mg/min.

options.t: Liposomal amphotericin B in normal saline
options.why: Saline breaks the liposomes; D5W only.

options.t: Ampicillin in D5W for a long infusion
Vancomycin in normal saline
Cefazolin in D5W

steps.q: Nitroglycerin infusion: which container?

options.t: Glass or polyolefin bag with non PVC tubing
Standard PVC bag with a 0.22 micron filter
options.why: Filters do not stop PVC absorption.

options.t: Amber PVC bag to protect from light
options.why: Light is not the main issue; PVC is.

options.t: Any bag, with a higher starting rate to compensate

cases.pearl: **Phenytoin NS only. Ampho B D5W only. Ampicillin NS. Nitro: no PVC.**

sources.t: St. Mary's IV room SOPs, BUD policy and competency program (verify locally)

cases.title: Parenteral nutrition: calcium and phosphate
cases.stem: You are checking an adult PN order with high calcium and phosphate.

steps.q: What is the main precipitation risk?

options.t: Calcium phosphate crystals in lung vessels
Lipid emulsion breaking (oiling out)
Vitamin breakdown from light exposure
Dextrose caramelizing inside the bag

steps.q: Which filter for a 3 in 1 PN (lipids in the bag)?

options.t: 1.2 micron filter
0.22 micron filter
5 micron filter
options.why: Used for some drugs drawn from ampules (filter needles), not PN.

options.t: No filter needed with lipids

steps.q: What osmolarity limit applies for peripheral PN?

options.t: About 900 mOsm/L or less
About 1,500 mOsm/L or less
About 600 mOsm/L or less
No limit if the IV is in a large vein

cases.pearl: **PN: watch Ca and Phos. 1.2 micron for lipids. Peripheral 900 mOsm/L max.**

sources.t: ASPEN parenteral nutrition safety consensus (Ayers P, et al. JPEN 2014;38:296-333)
St. Mary's IV room SOPs, BUD policy and competency program (verify locally)

cases.title: Final check of a CSP
cases.stem: A technician hands you a finished potassium chloride bag for your final check.

steps.q: What do you verify?

options.t: What went in: vials, pull back, images or weight
Full label: patient, drug, concentration, volume, BUD
Visual check for particles, cloudiness, leaks
The technician's confirmation that it is right
The patient's insurance coverage

steps.q: The label says 40 mEq in 100 mL "for peripheral use." What is wrong?

options.t: Central concentration; peripheral max about 10 mEq/h
It needs a 1.2 micron in line filter added
options.why: Filter choice is not the problem.

options.t: KCl must be mixed in D5W rather than NS
Nothing; the label wording is cosmetic

cases.pearl: **Final check: what went in, the label, and a look at the bag.**

cases.title: Shift simulation: IV room at 0600
cases.stem: At 0600: (1) a first dose cefepime for a septic patient; (2) the morning batch of 40 routine piggybacks; (3) your hood certification sticker expired yesterday; (4) a TPN due at 2100.

steps.q: What is the problem you must solve before compounding anything?

options.t: Certification lapsed: tell the supervisor, follow the SOP
options.why: Compounding in an uncertified hood violates USP 797.

options.t: Nothing: certification is paperwork only
options.why: It proves the air is clean.

options.t: Run a surface sample, then compound if clean
options.why: A surface sample does not replace certification.

options.t: Compound only Category 2 products until recertified

steps.q: Then what goes first?

options.t: The first dose cefepime for sepsis
The TPN that is due at 2100
The morning batch of 40 piggybacks
Restocking the hood for the day

cases.pearl: **Clean air first, then first doses, then batch, then later items.**
